# Matrix exponentials and commutators

Power series define matrix exponentials. Differentiating products of exponentials produces nested commutators.

Consider the *matrix-valued function* $$f(t) = e^{-tA} B e^{tA},$$ where $A$ and $B$ are square matrices. The matrix exponential is defined in terms of the Taylor series, $$\exp(X) = \mathbf{1} + X + \frac{1}{2!} X^2 + \frac{1}{3!} X^3 + \cdots,$$ which is convergent. It is a fact that if $XY-YX=[X,Y]=0$ (commuting matrices) then $\exp(X+Y) = \exp(X) \exp(Y)$, by the same proof as for the exponential function over a field $\mathbb{F}$.

## Solutions

### Tutor note: Taylor polynomials

**Tutor note:** I think it is important in quantum chemistry to be able to view matrices as vectors and as function parameters. On the other hand, some of this exercise may be hard for the student.

The first source item supplied the setup but no question, so it now appears in the chapter introduction.

### Solution to @exr-matrix-exponentials-and-commutators-explain-why-may-view-vector-valued {.unnumbered}

Identification of $\mathbb{F}^{n\times m}$ with $\mathbb{F}^{nm}$.

### Solution to @exr-matrix-exponentials-and-commutators-differentiable {.unnumbered}

Since $tA$ and $hA$ commute,

$$
e^{(t+h)A}=e^{tA}e^{hA}
=e^{tA}\left(\mathbf{1}+hA+O(h^2)\right).
$$

Therefore

$$
\lim_{h\to0}\frac{e^{(t+h)A}-e^{tA}}{h}=e^{tA}A=Ae^{tA}.
$$

### Solution to @exr-matrix-exponentials-and-commutators-differentiable-compute-its-derivatives-arbitrary-order {.unnumbered}

$f$ is a product of differentiable matrix-valued functions. The product rule gives

$$
f'(t)=[f(t),A].
$$

Repeated differentiation gives

$$
f^{(n)}(t)=\underbrace{[\cdots[[f(t),A],A],\ldots,A]}_{n\text{ commutators}}.
$$

:::
